title: Longest Mirror Subsequence
statement:
You get a string s of lowercase letters. Delete any number of characters (possibly none) without reordering the rest, so that what remains reads the same forwards and backwards.

Return the length of the longest such result. The kept characters do not have to be next to each other in s.

examples.why: Keep c, a, r, a, c (positions 0, 2, 3, 4, 5) to get "carac". The longest palindrome made of adjacent letters is only "ara", so a substring search gives the wrong answer.
No letter repeats, so the best you can keep is a single letter.
Drop the b: "mxaxm". The two outer m's are 5 positions apart, and they wrap the best answer for the middle "xaxb", which is "xax".

constraints: s contains only lowercase English letters
hints: Look at the first and the last character. What can you say when they are equal? And when they are not?
If s[i] === s[j], both can be kept as the outer pair, around the best answer for s[i+1..j-1]. If not, at least one of them is dropped.
Let best(i, j) be the answer for s[i..j]. Fill it for short ranges first, then longer ones: 2 + best(i+1, j-1) on a match, else max(best(i+1, j), best(i, j-1)).

explain.intuition:
Think about the two ends of the string. If s[i] and s[j] are the same letter, keeping both as the outermost pair never hurts: whatever palindrome you build inside can be wrapped by them. So the answer is 2 plus the answer for the inside. If they differ, they cannot both be the outer pair, so at least one end is dropped, and you take the better of the two choices.

That gives a recurrence over ranges [i, j], and every range depends only on shorter ranges inside it. There are about n²/2 ranges, so filling a table from short to long is O(n²). It is the same "two ends of an interval" shape as many interval DP problems; you can also see it as the longest common subsequence of s and its reverse.
steps: Let dp[i][j] be the answer for s[i..j]. Every single letter gives dp[i][i] = 1.
Go through i from n − 1 down to 0, and j from i + 1 up to n − 1, so the inner ranges are ready.
If s[i] === s[j]: dp[i][j] = 2 + dp[i+1][j−1] (with an empty inside counting as 0).
Return dp[0][n−1]. Only row i + 1 is needed to fill row i, so two 1-D arrays are enough.
pitfalls: Solving the substring version instead. The kept letters may be far apart, as in "character".
Wrong fill order: dp[i][j] needs dp[i+1][…], so i must go from the end backwards.
When j = i + 1 and the letters match, the inside is empty. Reading dp[i+1][i] must give 0, not garbage.

solutions.title: Plain recursion on the two ends
solutions.idea: Apply the recurrence directly without remembering results. Correct, but the same ranges are solved again and again, which blows up to about 2ⁿ calls.

solutions.title: Interval DP with two rows
solutions.idea: Fill answers for ranges from the back. Row i needs only row i + 1, so keep just those two rows.

followups: Return one longest palindromic subsequence itself, not just its length.
What is the fewest letters you must insert to turn s into a palindrome? How does it relate to this answer?
